orgs.name: Greater Chicago Food Depository
orgs.short: Supplies food to 850+ pantries, kitchens and shelters
orgs.why: Most Chicago food pantries get their food from the Depository.

orgs.name: Nourishing Hope
orgs.short: Food pantries and grocery delivery, plus counseling
orgs.why: Nourishing Hope puts therapists and caseworkers behind the same door as the groceries, because hunger rarely arrives alone.

orgs.name: Care for Real
orgs.short: Food pantries, clothing and home delivery
orgs.why: Ninety-three cents of every dollar reaches programs, the highest of any four-star organization in this guide, and it has run surpluses while expanding.

orgs.name: Beyond Hunger
orgs.short: Food pantry and home delivery in 13 ZIP codes
orgs.why: Beyond Hunger covers thirteen ZIP codes across Oak Park, River Forest, Forest Park, Berwyn and Chicago’s West Side, where need shows up as a quiet line at a church door and is easy to miss.

orgs.name: Common Pantry
orgs.short: Client-choice food pantry with hot meals
orgs.why: The oldest food pantry in this guide, and a client-choice one: people pick their own groceries off the shelf, the way anyone shops.

orgs.name: Cradles to Crayons
orgs.short: Clothing and essentials for children, through social services
orgs.why: Children outgrow coats faster than families can replace them, and there is no public program for that.

orgs.name: Literacy Chicago
orgs.short: Free adult literacy, ESL and GED classes
orgs.why: Adult literacy draws less attention than any cause in this guide and is among the most consequential: reading a lease or a prescription label affects a whole household.

orgs.name: Open Books
orgs.short: Bookstores that fund K–12 literacy programs
orgs.why: A used-bookstore chain that funds its own literacy programming, which is an elegant model and a fragile one.

orgs.name: Bernie’s Book Bank
orgs.short: Free books for kids, birth to sixth grade
orgs.why: The only organization in this guide whose core claim rests on a five-year randomized controlled trial — children who received books across multiple years gained roughly half to two-thirds of a typical school year’s reading growth, at twenty dollars a child.

orgs.name: Chicago Public Library Foundation
orgs.short: Funds library programs taxes do not cover
orgs.why: The library is the last free indoor public space in most neighborhoods.

orgs.name: One Million Degrees
orgs.short: Coaching and money for community college students
orgs.why: Community college completion is where the American education promise breaks — most students who enroll never finish.

orgs.name: Chicago Scholars
orgs.short: Mentors first-generation students to college and career
orgs.why: Chicago Scholars stays with first-generation students through college and into a first job, past the easier step of getting admitted.

orgs.name: After School Matters
orgs.short: Paid after-school apprenticeships for high school teens
orgs.why: Teenagers get paid to do the work — arts, STEM, sports, media — which reframes the whole thing from enrichment to employment.

orgs.name: All Chicago Making Homelessness History
orgs.short: Coordinates the homelessness response and emergency aid
orgs.why: This is the coordinating layer for Chicago’s entire homelessness response, and its emergency fund pays the rent gap that turns a bad month into an eviction.

orgs.name: Chicago Coalition to End Homelessness
orgs.short: Homelessness policy, organizing and legal aid
orgs.why: The coalition writes the bills, sues, and forces the counts that shelters and city agencies then argue over.

orgs.name: La Casa Norte
orgs.short: Shelter and housing for homeless youth and families
orgs.why: Youth homelessness is mostly hidden: young people tend to couch-surf, which keeps them out of the counts.

orgs.name: The Night Ministry
orgs.short: Overnight outreach, street medicine and youth shelter
orgs.why: Two things nobody else does at this hour: a bus that finds people where they already are, and a nurse on it.

orgs.name: Deborah’s Place
orgs.short: Supportive housing for women who are homeless
orgs.why: The only organization in this guide built specifically for women who are homeless alone: without children, and so outside most of the family shelter system.

orgs.name: Breakthrough
orgs.short: Shelter, housing and services in one neighborhood
orgs.why: Everything in one forty-block stretch of East Garfield Park: shelters, housing, a fresh-food market, schools programming, behavioral health.

orgs.name: Franciscan Outreach
orgs.short: Chicago’s largest interim shelters
orgs.why: Chicago’s largest interim shelters — 263,000 meals and 99,000 shelter nights in a year, run out of three buildings on the West and Southwest Sides.

orgs.name: National Immigrant Justice Center
orgs.short: Legal representation for immigrants and asylum seekers
orgs.why: Deportation is the only major American legal process where you can lose everything without a lawyer, because there is no right to appointed counsel.

orgs.name: The Resurrection Project
orgs.short: Affordable housing and immigration legal services
orgs.why: The Resurrection Project has bought and built affordable housing in Pilsen since 1990, and adds immigration legal services and homeownership counseling.

orgs.name: Legal Aid Chicago
orgs.short: Free civil legal help for people in poverty
orgs.why: Eviction court moves faster than tenants can learn the rules, and most landlords arrive with counsel while most tenants do not.

orgs.name: Invisible Institute
orgs.short: Police accountability journalism and public records
orgs.why: Three Pulitzer Prizes in four years, from a team of about a dozen people on the South Side, for reporting on police misconduct and missing persons cases nobody else was doing.

orgs.name: Chicago Votes Education Fund
orgs.short: Registers young and incarcerated voters
orgs.why: They made Cook County Jail the first jail-based polling place in the country, then registered more than 11,000 people inside it.

orgs.name: Chicago CRED
orgs.short: Outreach, therapy and jobs for men at highest risk
orgs.why: The strongest evidence in Chicago gun violence work: men who finished the full two-year program were 73 percent less likely to be arrested for a violent crime, in a Northwestern study published in PNAS.

orgs.name: Institute for Nonviolence Chicago
orgs.short: Street outreach and violence interruption
orgs.why: Violence interruption is the work of knowing who is about to shoot whom and getting there first, which requires people the street trusts more than it trusts police.

orgs.name: Youth Guidance
orgs.short: School counseling programs, including Becoming A Man
orgs.why: Becoming A Man has the best evidence of anything in this guide: four randomized controlled trials that pool to a reduction of up to 37 percent in violent-crime arrests, at a benefit-cost ratio between two and ten to one.

orgs.name: Cara Collective
orgs.short: Job training and placement for people facing barriers
orgs.why: A staffing business and a job-training program inside one organization, so participants work for real wages before they interview anywhere else.

orgs.name: Metropolitan Family Services
orgs.short: Family services and violence intervention region-wide
orgs.why: A hundred and sixty-nine years old, $180 million a year, and the coordinator of violence intervention across 24 Chicago neighborhoods.

orgs.name: Chicago Children’s Advocacy Center
orgs.short: One place where abused children get help
orgs.why: Before this existed, a child who had been abused told the story to an investigator, then a detective, then a doctor, then a prosecutor.

orgs.name: Howard Brown Health
orgs.short: Health center focused on LGBTQ+ patients
orgs.why: Half a century of providing care to LGBTQ+ Chicagoans, much of it during years when nobody else would, now serving 47,000 patients across seven clinics regardless of ability to pay.

orgs.name: Erie Family Health Centers
orgs.short: Community health centers, regardless of ability to pay
orgs.why: Fourteen clinics from the West Side to Waukegan, 95,000 patients, 90 percent of them low-income, and no deficit year since 2019.

orgs.name: Chicago Foundation for Women
orgs.short: Grants to groups serving women and girls
orgs.why: A regrantor, which means it does the diligence on small organizations you would never find yourself and moves money to them — $55 million across 5,500 grants since 1985.

orgs.name: Apna Ghar
orgs.short: Crisis support for immigrant survivors of violence
orgs.why: A domestic violence shelter is only usable if you can be understood inside it.

orgs.name: Connections for Abused Women and their Children
orgs.short: Hotline, shelter and advocacy for domestic violence survivors
orgs.why: Nineteen thousand nights of safe refuge, plus advocates stationed inside Stroger and Northwestern emergency rooms — the place where an injury is often the first disclosure.

orgs.name: Friends of the Chicago River
orgs.short: Cleanups and restoration for the Chicago River
orgs.why: The river was an industrial sewer within living memory and is now swimmable in places, which happened because a small organization has refused to let it go since 1979.

orgs.name: Openlands
orgs.short: Protects open space and plants urban trees
orgs.why: Land conservation in a metro area means buying the thing before someone else builds on it, which is expensive, unglamorous and permanent.

orgs.name: Urban Growers Collective
orgs.short: Urban farms, youth jobs and a mobile market
orgs.why: Eight farms on the South and West Sides, which is a food access project and a jobs project at once — 205 teenagers were paid to grow food last year.

causes.query: immigration defense, civil legal aid and police accountability

causes.label: Violence prevention and youth
causes.query: gun violence prevention and youth development

causes.query: community health centers and free clinics

causes.label: Women and survivors
causes.query: domestic violence services and women’s funds

randomized-trial.label: Randomized trial
randomized-trial.gloss: Tested against a control group. The strongest evidence available for social programs.

independent-study.label: Independent study
independent-study.gloss: Evaluated by an outside researcher. Includes studies the organization commissioned itself.

self-reported.label: Self-reported
self-reported.gloss: Counted by the organization itself. No outside evaluation of the program’s effect is on file here.
